endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: AI systems should be developed and evaluated with a specific focus on mitigating bias and promoting health equity, ensuring that the deployment of these technologies does not exacerbate existing disparities

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: In case of an adverse event or large-scale issue, determine whether there is a clearly defined, unbiased (to business interests), and easy-to-access 60 way that affected individuals or groups can provide feedback or seek guidance, and whether these processes are consistent with state and federal policies.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Assess safety to physical environments when deploying GAI systems.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The HDO is transparent that some AI uses are not eligible for opt-out, and explains why in accessible terms.

endorsements.title: How AI can learn from the law: putting humans in the loop only on appeal
endorsements.quote: For example, companies developing or using AI/ML systems can setup specialized processes and teams to review appeal requests from end users or anyone affected by the AI/ML decisions—similar to customer support but focusing instead on specific AI/ML decisions and not on, say, product repairs or returns.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether patient or caregiver mechanisms to request clinician review, appeal, or contest AI-influenced decisions reduce uncorrected errors, and no supplied study documents how often the hazard occurs. Support for R241 rests on five guidance, framework, and commentary sources, and only two of their quoted passages address appeal or feedback channels directly.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. All five endorsements are guidance, frameworks, or commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the size of any benefit remains unknown.

All five sources use "should" language, but only the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide and the appeal-focused commentary describe feedback or appeal routes. The CHAI guide asks that such routes be unbiased to business interests and consistent with state and federal policy. The quoted augmented intelligence principles and NIST AI 600-1 passages address bias and physical safety, not appeals.

The CHAI guide calls for an easy-to-access way for affected people to seek guidance, and the CHAI playbook asks organizations to explain in accessible terms when opt-out is unavailable. No supplied study measures whether patients know these routes exist, use them, or reach a licensed clinician through them.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare decision reversal rates, time to clinician review, and downstream harm between settings with and without patient-facing appeal mechanisms for AI-influenced care and coverage decisions. Studies should also measure how often patients use such mechanisms and how accessible patients find them.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The groups who may face the greatest barriers to filing an appeal remain unstudied, and no study has checked in any population whether these mechanisms are as accessible as the sources call for.
